documents.source: The Tax Favored By Most Economists

chunks.text: Unlike most taxes, carbon taxation can correct a market failure and make the economy more efficient.
Economists have long recommended a tax on fossil-fuel energy sources as an efficient way to address this problem.
Most analyses find that a carbon tax could significantly reduce emissions.
As one of the few taxes favored by economists, carbon taxes could help the nation address several issues simultaneously.

documents.source: The Case Against a Carbon Tax

metadata.author: Jordan McGillis, Institute for Energy Research

chunks.text: Carbon taxes are nonobjective, they are coercive, and they are impediments to prosperity.
Americans in the lowest income quintile use a greater percentage of their income to meet their energy needs than the remainder of Americans, rendering carbon taxes regressive.
Carbon taxes slow economic growth unless a large portion of the tax revenue is allocated to corporate tax reductions.
The U.S. is only responsible for around 15 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions.

documents.source: How can nuclear combat climate change?

chunks.text: Combating climate change would be much harder, without an increased role for nuclear in achieving the deep decarbonization required to keep global temperature rise below 1.5C.
Nuclear power plants produce no greenhouse gas emissions during operation, and over its life-cycle nuclear produces about the same emissions per unit of electricity as wind.
Because nuclear power is reliable and can be deployed on a large scale, it can directly replace fossil fuel plant, avoiding the combustion of fossil fuels for electricity generation.
The use of nuclear energy today avoids emissions roughly equivalent to removing one-third of all cars from the world's roads.

documents.source: Does Nuclear Power Slow Or Speed Climate Change?

chunks.text: Building new reactors, or operating most existing ones, makes climate change worse compared with spending the same money on more-climate-effective ways to deliver the same energy services.
New nuclear plants will save many-fold less carbon per dollar than competing carbon-free resources, in proportion to their relative costs.
Being both slower and costlier than its modern competitors makes nuclear power doubly unhelpful for protecting the climate.
Nuclear plants take many years to build, typically around a decade, while renewable projects can take a year or less.

documents.source: Why We Can't Afford to Dismiss Carbon Offsetting

metadata.author: Bronson Griscom, Conservation International (via The Nature Conservancy)

chunks.text: Carbon offsets are essential because they provide a simple way to keep, improve and expand forests.
Nature can deliver a third of the emissions cuts needed by 2030 to avert climate disaster.
Carbon markets create positive incentives that upend the conventional economic motivations that render tropical forests more valuable dead than alive.
High-quality forest carbon projects provide the financing needed to ensure governments and local communities keep their forests standing.

documents.source: Revealed: more than 90% of rainforest carbon offsets by biggest provider are worthless, analysis shows

chunks.text: More than 90 percent of the rainforest offset credits are likely to be phantom credits and do not represent genuine carbon reductions.
Companies are using credits to make claims of reducing emissions when most of these credits don't represent emissions reductions at all.
Credits from 21 projects had no climate benefit, and seven had between 98 percent and 52 percent fewer than claimed using Verra's system.
The offset market is broken.

documents.source: Outgrowing growth: why quality of life, not GDP, should be our measure of success

chunks.text: If we want a decent shot at climate stability, high-income nations will have to shift to post-growth economic principles.
By reducing the material 'throughput' of our economy - the amount of stuff we produce and consume - we can reduce our energy demand.
The less energy we use, the easier it is to accomplish a rapid transition to renewables.
We can accomplish our social goals right now, without any growth at all, simply by sharing what we already have more fairly.

documents.source: People are realizing that degrowth is bad

chunks.text: Degrowth is a non-starter, and green growth won't happen fast enough on its own.
Demanding that people in rich countries accept absolutely catastrophic declines in their living standards is a political non-starter.
The claim that economic growth requires growth in resource use is false; rich countries have started to grow while using less of the planet's most important resources.
Rapid decarbonization, curbing of global pollution, and resource conservation are tall orders, but unlike degrowth, they are possible.

documents.source: "Global Divestment Day" Challenges Fossil Fuel Industry on February 13-14

chunks.text: Divestment serves as a key tool in moving the world beyond fossil fuels and towards renewable energy.
An Oxford University research called the effort the fastest growing divestment campaign in history, one that could have a far reaching impact on the industry's bottom line.
The fossil fuel divestment movement has grown exponentially over the last two years - now it's going global.
Over twenty colleges and universities, dozens of religious institutions, and numerous cities have committed to divest, representing over USD 50 billion in assets.

documents.source: Fossil fuel divestment could prove counterproductive to curbing carbon emissions

metadata.author: Andrew Fawthrop (quoting Stefan Andreasson), NS Energy Business

chunks.text: The divestment movement will simply force IOCs to cede market share to NOCs, and if anything this would cause CO2 emissions to rise.
The push for oil and gas divestment is likely to have unintended consequences.
IOCs are generally better placed and more willing than are NOCs to reduce the carbon intensity of their products and support the transition to renewable energy.
The divestment movement will transfer the supply of fossil fuel to companies that are more polluting, less transparent, and less committed to addressing the climate crisis.

documents.source: Toward a Responsible Solar Geoengineering Research Program

chunks.text: The potential benefits of solar geoengineering warrant a large-scale international research effort.
Uncertainty is real, but it speaks louder as an argument for rather than against research.
Each of these concerns has merit, but they do not, individually or collectively, amount to a strong argument against research.
A project large enough to cut the economic damage in half could be implemented at a cost of a few billion dollars per year, several hundred times less than the damage it would prevent.

documents.source: We Call for an International Non-Use Agreement on Solar Geoengineering

metadata.author: Frank Biermann et al. (Solar Geoengineering Non-Use Agreement Initiative)

chunks.text: Solar geoengineering is not necessary, desirable, ethical, or politically governable in the current context.
The risks of solar geoengineering are poorly understood and can never be fully known.
Speculative hopes about the future availability of solar geoengineering technologies threaten commitments to mitigation and can disincentivize governments.
Without effective global and democratic controls, the geopolitics of possible unilateral deployment of solar geoengineering would be frightening and inequitable.

documents.source: A Plan to Power 100 Percent of the Planet with Renewables

metadata.author: Mark Z. Jacobson and Mark A. Delucchi

chunks.text: A large-scale wind, water and solar energy system can reliably supply the world's needs, significantly benefiting climate, air quality, water quality, ecology and energy security.
The mix of WWS sources in our plan can reliably supply the residential, commercial, industrial and transportation sectors.
Interconnecting wind farms that are only 100 to 200 miles apart can compensate for hours of zero power at any one farm should the wind not be blowing there.
Because the wind often blows during stormy conditions when the sun does not shine, combining wind and solar can go a long way toward meeting demand.

documents.source: Any Green New Deal Is Dead Without Nuclear Power

chunks.text: Renewables alone cannot meet the goal of decarbonizing the world economy.
The nuclear and hydro are needed, in place of natural gas, for baseload power and to load-follow the enormous amount of renewables.
We don't have a century, and if so many new gas plants are built to load-follow wind and solar, then we lock ourselves into gas for a long, long time.
No one is going to decommission or destroy a relatively new gas plant.

documents.source: Natural Gas: A Bridge Fuel for the 21st Century

metadata.author: John Podesta and Timothy E. Wirth, Center for American Progress

chunks.text: Natural gas can serve as a bridge fuel to a 21st-century energy economy that relies on efficiency, renewable sources, and low-carbon fossil fuels.
Natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel - it produces less than half as much carbon pollution as coal.
Recent technology advancements make affordable the development of unconventional natural gas resources.
This creates an unprecedented opportunity to use gas as a bridge fuel to a 21st-century energy economy.

documents.source: Burning the Gas 'Bridge Fuel' Myth: Why Gas Is Not Clean, Cheap, or Necessary

chunks.text: The myth of gas as a 'bridge' to a stable climate does not stand up to scrutiny.
Multibillion-dollar gas infrastructure built today is designed to operate for decades to come, locking in emissions.
Further development of untapped gas reserves is inconsistent with the climate goals in the Paris Agreement.
Given the barriers to closing down infrastructure ahead of its expected economic lifespan, it is critical to stop building new infrastructure.

documents.source: Can We Afford a Green New Deal?

chunks.text: The problem is austerity bias; for whatever reason governments refuse to spend even when the economic case for it is overwhelming.
When interest rates are below GDP growth rates, the debt-to-GDP ratio stabilizes on its own, even if you run deficits forever.
By any measure, the US economy has operated below potential for the large majority of the time in recent decades.
Climate change may be a crisis urgent enough to overcome the entrenched austerity bias of governments.

documents.source: Why the U.S. Can't Afford a Green New Deal

metadata.author: Jeffrey Miron and Laura Nicolae, Cato Institute

chunks.text: Given that the US cannot afford its existing entitlement programs, adopting the massively expensive policies proposed by Democratic candidates would be foolish.
Federal debt held by the public, currently at 78 percent of GDP, will approach 100 percent in the next decade and reach 152 percent by 2048.
The Green New Deal would likely cost upwards of $6.6 trillion per year.
Even if the US adopted all three of these new taxes, annual federal revenue would increase by at most $280 billion.

documents.source: Putting progress over protectionism in climate policy

chunks.text: Such reciprocity serves as a useful enforcement mechanism for global emissions reductions rather than mere protectionism.

The CBAM counteracts the competitive disadvantage to local firms from carbon pricing, avoiding the possibility that European consumers would choose lower cost dirty imports over cleaner domestic alternatives.
The European approach is nondiscriminatory, asking trading partners to bear the same costs that domestic companies face when serving the European market.
As more countries join such efforts, the rest of the world has an incentive to adopt carbon pricing to avoid tariffs on their exports.

documents.source: Are Carbon Border Adjustments a Dream Climate Policy or Protectionist Nightmare?

chunks.text: At worst, they are disguised economic protectionism providing avenues for rent seeking and cronyism.
A carbon tariff system or CBAM could serve as a vehicle for protecting special interests - not the environment - at the expense of American businesses, consumers, and the economy.
These policies are likely to create uneven distributional effects on consumers as well as multiple pathways for rent seeking, cronyism, and protectionism.
It makes little sense to base a potentially damaging and far-reaching policy on an idea that lacks clear empirical support and scholarly consensus.
